title: Sourdough
wiki_lead: Sourdough is a leavening agent containing naturally occurring yeast and lactobacillus bacteria. The term is used to describe bread baked with sourdough, while the sourdough itself is referred to as a starter.  In addition to leavening the bread, the fermentation process produces lactic acid, which gives the bread its distinctive sour taste and improves its keeping qualities.
wiki_excerpt:
Sourdough is a leavening agent containing naturally occurring yeast and lactobacillus bacteria. The term is used to describe bread baked with sourdough, while the sourdough itself is referred to as a starter.  In addition to leavening the bread, the fermentation process produces lactic acid, which gives the bread its distinctive sour taste and improves its keeping qualities.


History
Sourdough is one of the most ancient and popular forms of leavening bread. It was the standard method of breadmaking for most of human history until the Middle Ages, when it was replaced by barm. Barm, in turn, was replaced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by industrially produced baker's yeast.
The Encyclopedia of Food Microbiology states: "One of the oldest sourdough breads dates from 3700 BC and was excavated in Switzerland, but the origin of sourdough fermentation likely relates to the origin of agriculture in the Fertile Crescent and Egypt several thousand years earlier", and "Bread production relied on the use of sourdough as a leavening agent for most of human history; the use of baker's yeast as a leavening agent dates back less than 150 years from the year of 2014". Pliny the Elder described several methods of sourdough leavening to make bread. Sourdough remained the usual form of leavening down into the European Middle Ages until being replaced by barm from the beer-brewing process, and after 1871 by purpose-cultured yeast.
French bakers brought sourdough techniques to Northern California during the California Gold Rush, and it remains a part of the culture of San Francisco today. (The nickname remains in "Sourdough Sam", the mascot of the San Francisco 49ers.) Sourdough has long been associated with the 1849 gold prospectors, though they were more likely to make bread with commercial yeast or baking soda. The "celebrated" San Francisco sourdough is a white bread characterized by a pronounced sourness, and indeed the strain of Lactobacillus in sourdough starters is named Fructilactobacillus sanfranciscensis (previously Lactobacillus sanfranciscensis), alongside the sourdough yeast Kasachstania humilis (previously Candida milleri) found in the same cultures.
The sourdough tradition was carried into the Department of Alaska in the United States and the Yukon Territory in Canada during the Klondike Gold Rush of 1898. Conventional leavenings, such as yeast and baking soda, were much less reliable in the conditions faced by the prospectors. Experienced miners and other settlers frequently carried a pouch of starter either around their neck or on a belt; these were fiercely guarded to keep them from freezing. However, freezing does not kill a sourdough starter; excessive heat does. Old hands came to be called "sourdoughs", a term that is still applied to any Alaskan or Klondike old-timer. The significance of the nickname's association with Yukon culture was immortalized in the writings of Robert Service, particularly his collection of "Songs of a Sourdo
grok_lead: Sourdough is a fermented dough consisting of flour and water, leavened naturally by a symbiotic culture of wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria rather than commercial baker's yeast. This process produces a tangy flavor, chewy texture, and extended shelf life due to the production of organic acids and enzymes during fermentation. Unlike conventional bread, sourdough relies on spontaneous microbial activity from the environment and flour, resulting in a diverse microbiome that varies by region and ingredients. The history of sourdough dates back over 4,000 years to ancient Egypt, where it emerged as one of the earliest forms of leavened bread through accidental fermentation of dough mixtures. It spread across cultures, including in Europe and the Americas, where it became a staple for miners during the 19th-century California Gold Rush, earning the nickname "sourdoughs" for prospectors who carried starters in their kits. Today, sourdough has seen a global resurgence, driven by interest in artisanal baking and its perceived health benefits, with the market projected to reach USD 4.49 billion by 2030 at a CAGR of 6.68% as of 2025. At its core, sourdough fermentation involves maintaining a "starter" cultureâa thick mixture of flour and water, often initiated with rye flour for its nutrient density and ability to accelerate fermentation, refreshed periodically to propagate microbes such as Lactobacillus species (e.g., L. sanfranciscensis) and yeasts like Saccharomyces cerevisiae or Kazachstania exigua. These microorganisms break down starches into lactic and acetic acids, carbon dioxide for rising, and other compounds that enhance flavor and digestibility. Fermentation times vary considerably depending on the method, ingredients, and conditions. Traditional processes often span 12â24 hours or longer, whereas many contemporary home recipesâparticularly those using refined all-purpose flourâemploy shorter bulk fermentation periods of 3â6 hours, facilitated by higher starter inoculation rates, warmer proofing temperatures (typically 74â78Â°F or 23â26Â°C), and techniques such as periodic stretch-and-folds to rapidly develop gluten structure. This variation is influenced by factors like temperature (ideally 20â30Â°C), flour type (e.g., hard wheat varieties such as hard red wheat for nutty flavor and strong gluten, hard white wheat for milder flavor similar to commercial bread flour and high protein content of 11-14% for excellent gluten development and structure, rye for faster fermentation and tangy flavor, whole grain for more acidity, ancient grains like spelt, einkorn, and emmer for unique nutty or sweet flavors and nutrition but often best blended with wheat for better rise and texture, or barley for distinct flavor profiles), and hydration level, yielding breads with a lower glycemic index and improved nutrient bioavailability compared to yeasted counterparts, with these advantagesâalong with more complex flavor profilesâbeing more pronounced in longer fermentation durations that enable greater production of organic acids, formation of resistant starch, and degradation of phytic acid compared to shorter processes that yield milder results closer to conventionally yeasted loaves. Beyond baking, sourdough offers nutritional advantages, including reduced levels of FODMAPs (by 65â75% in some cases), increased resistant starch (up to 120%), and better mineral absorption like iron (by 10%) and zinc (by 25%), making it suitable for those with sensitivities. Its antimicrobial properties from acids and peptides also extend shelf life by inhibiting mold growth. Culturally, sourdough symbolizes resilience and tradition, with ongoing research exploring its microbiome for innovations in gluten-free and fortified breads.
